title: Session affinity and conversation routing - architecture review notes
content:
Meeting date: 2025-02-11
Attendees: Priya (chair), Marco, Gabrielle, Samir, Hannah, Alex (notes)
Context / problem statement:
- As more customers build multi-turn conversational products, we need predictable latency and consistent model state for active conversations. Current strategy routes every request independently (stateless routing) which causes KV cache misses and state rehydration when requests hit different worker pools. That leads to tail latency spikes and inconsistent token-costs per conversation.
- We need an architecture for session affinity (sticky routing) that balances: per-conversation state locality, autoscaling elasticity, multi-tenant isolation, and operational simplicity across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.
Agenda:
1) Proposed affinity keys and routing layers
2) Tradeoffs: latency vs utilization vs isolation
3) Failure modes and graceful degradation
4) Action items and follow-ups

Summary of proposals discussed:
A. Conversation-ID sticky routing (preferred initial approach)
  - Use an incoming conversation_id (client-provided) or derive from the first-turn seed to compute a stable routing key. Hash -> ring -> pinned worker pool (soft-pin for X minutes).
  - Soft-pin TTL: default 15 minutes of inactivity; configurable per-customer.
  - Affinity applies at worker-pool granularity, not individual GPU core; allows batching inside pool.
  - Pros: predictable locality (KV cache warm), lower tail latency for active conversations, simpler rollback to stateless routing.
  - Cons: uneven load if conversation distribution skewed; requires eviction/reshuffle when pool scales down.

B. Token-hash probabilistic affinity (fallback/alternative)
  - Hash request tokens + client id to probabilistically route to same GPU family but not exact worker. Intended for extremely high-cardinality workloads to avoid heavy skew.
  - Pros: smoother utilization; easier to autoscale.
  - Cons: weaker guarantees for KV cache locality; still causes extra misses.

C. Lease-based session ownership (for Dedicated/Private)
  - Lease record in distributed metadata store (etcd/consul/our control plane) indicating a session owner worker id and lease TTL. Renew on each request. If lease lost, another node can steal.
  - Pros: strong single-writer guarantee, better for privacy/isolation for customers demanding strict tenancy.
  - Cons: operational complexity, increased latency on lease checks, hard for Hosted at scale.

Decisions made during meeting:
- Move forward with approach A (Conversation-ID sticky routing) as the default for Hosted and Dedicated, with configurable TTL and a clear opt-out to stateless routing for customers who prefer distribution. Rationale: best balance of latency improvements and implementation complexity; minimizes control-plane load compared to leases.
- Implement probabilistic token-hash routing (approach B) as an optional routing policy for extremely high-throughput customers where utilization fairness is prioritized.
- Reserve lease-based ownership (approach C) as an enterprise-only feature behind Dedicated/Private offering - will be a tracked follow-up RFC for integration with the control plane.

Key design constraints & notes:
- Affinity must be enforced at the API gateway/routing layer before batching decisions to avoid mixing conversations across pools.
- Worker pools must expose a lightweight health + capacity signal (score: free_slots + recent_cpu_pct) so routing can avoid directing new conversations to saturated pools.
- On scale-up, the routing layer should prefer cold-start new conversations on new capacity to avoid overloading nodes holding many warm sessions.
- On scale-down, the controller will perform TTL-based spillover: sessions pinned to evicting pool get marked for proactive rehash to new pool with prioritized cache pre-warming (see action items).

Failure modes and mitigations:
1) Hot-key / skewed conversation owners -> overload single pool
   - Mitigation: adaptive split: detect hot-session by request rate per conversation_id and allow dynamic sharding (split into sub-keys based on a sequence number or sub-hash). Provide per-conversation throttling and backpressure policies.
2) Node failure with many pinned sessions -> sudden rehydration storm
   - Mitigation: staggered reassignments, prioritized cache priming for highest-traffic sessions, temporary elevated batching window for first N requests to absorb spike.
3) Control-plane latency causing misrouted requests
   - Mitigation: routing layer caches affinity map with short TTL and fallback to deterministic hash if control-plane unreachable.

Operational considerations:
- Observability: introduce session-level metrics in Console -> active_sessions_per_pool, session_stickiness_ttl, session_reassign_rate, average_cache_miss_after_reassign. Add alert when session_reassign_rate > threshold.
- Cost: affinity increases effective hot-working-set on specific GPUs; need to surface expected delta in token-cost per customer in Redwood Console.
- Security/privacy: ensure conversation_id hashing uses tenant-salted hash so same raw id across tenants does not map to same worker. Consider HMAC with tenant secret.

Action items (owners and tentative due dates):
- Prototype routing shim in edge-proxy that consumes conversation_id and resolves pool ring (Marco) — prototype by 2025-02-20
- Autoscaler integration: policy for preferring new conversation placement on new nodes and graceful drain behavior (Gabrielle) — draft by 2025-02-24
- Cache priming API: endpoint for controller to pre-warm KV cache for transferred sessions + prioritized token prefetch mechanism (Samir) — spike and bench by 2025-02-28
- Console metrics: add session-level metrics & dashboard (Hannah) — basic dashboard by 2025-03-03
- Security review: tenant-salted hashing / HMAC pattern and guidance for customers (Priya + Security) — review meeting 2025-02-18
- Follow-up RFC for lease-based ownership (approach C) scoped to Dedicated/Private (Priya) — RFC draft by 2025-03-10

Open questions (to resolve in follow-ups):
- Default TTL sizing: 15m was the working default, but we need real workload telemetry to tune. Where do we surface per-customer overrides?
- How to measure the tradeoff in unit costs precisely? Need a synthetic workload that simulates conversation churn.
- For session split (hot-key mitigation), what is the client-visible contract? Will splitting change conversation id semantics? Prefer server-side sub-keying but need API compatibility check.

Notes on benchmarks discussed:
- Marco presented a micro-bench showing 2.3x reduction in 99thpct latency for multi-turn flows when session affinity is maintained vs fully stateless under same load (toy model, small sample). We need larger-scale tests using real customer traces.

Appendix / references:
- Related tickets: CR-5721 (request routing telemetry), CR-5807 (autoscaler drain behavior), PR-1889 (edge-proxy routing shim initial commit)
- Next meeting: architecture sync 2025-02-18 to review prototype results and security guidance.

Meeting notes recorded by Alex.
